summary.text: At \(n=140\), the bounds \(4k^2\le 5n^2<4(k+1)^2\) determine the relevant square-root floors and give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus the proposed identity would assert \(542=528+484-471=541\), providing a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(m)=2m+\left\lfloor m\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac m4\right\rfloor
\qquad(m\ge 1).
\]
We will disprove the proposed recurrence by evaluating it at a single index, namely \(n=140\).

First, we record a convenient way to determine the irrational floor term. For nonnegative integers \(m\) and \(k\), if
\[
4k^2\le 5m^2<4(k+1)^2,
\]
then
\[
\left\lfloor m\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=k.
\]
Indeed, all the quantities involved are nonnegative, and
\[
\left(m\sqrt{\frac54}\right)^2=\frac{5m^2}{4}.
\]
Thus \(4k^2\le 5m^2\) implies
\[
k^2\le \left(m\sqrt{\frac54}\right)^2,
\]
and hence \(k\le m\sqrt{5/4}\). Similarly, \(5m^2<4(k+1)^2\) implies
\[
\left(m\sqrt{\frac54}\right)^2<(k+1)^2,
\]
so \(m\sqrt{5/4}<k+1\). Consequently
\[
k\le m\sqrt{\frac54}<k+1,
\]
which is exactly the assertion that the floor is \(k\).

We now use this criterion at the four arguments appearing in the recurrence for \(n=140\).

For \(m=161\), take \(k=180\). The required integer comparisons are
\[
4\cdot 180^2=4\cdot 32400=129600,
\]
\[
5\cdot 161^2=5\cdot 25921=129605,
\]
and
\[
4\cdot 181^2=4\cdot 32761=131044.
\]
Therefore
\[
129600\le129605<131044,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
Also \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Hence
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

For \(m=157\), take \(k=175\). Here
\[
4\cdot175^2=4\cdot30625=122500,
\]
\[
5\cdot157^2=5\cdot24649=123245,
\]
and
\[
4\cdot176^2=4\cdot30976=123904.
\]
Thus
\[
122500\le123245<123904,
\]
and consequently
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Since \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\), we obtain
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

For \(m=144\), take \(k=160\). We have
\[
4\cdot160^2=4\cdot25600=102400,
\]
\[
5\cdot144^2=5\cdot20736=103680,
\]
and
\[
4\cdot161^2=4\cdot25921=103684.
\]
Therefore
\[
102400\le103680<103684,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Moreover, \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\). It follows that
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

Finally, for \(m=140\), take \(k=156\). The comparisons are
\[
4\cdot156^2=4\cdot24336=97344,
\]
\[
5\cdot140^2=5\cdot19600=98000,
\]
and
\[
4\cdot157^2=4\cdot24649=98596.
\]
Hence
\[
97344\le98000<98596,
\]
which gives
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\), and therefore
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

The conjecture claims that for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n).
\]
Substituting \(n=140\), which is an allowed index, would require
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
The exact values computed above turn this equation into
\[
542=528+484-471.
\]
But
\[
528+484-471=1012-471=541,
\]
so the required equality would be \(542=541\), which is false.

Thus the proposed recurrence fails at \(n=140\). Therefore it is not true that
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
for every \(n\ge1\), and the conjecture is disproved.
